analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1% federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the 1% tax that public companies pay when they buy back their own stock was introduced with zero cosponsors on January 23, 2025 and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without any action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the 1% excise tax that publicly traded companies currently pay on the fair market value of stock they repurchase, a tax Congress created in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 [S2][S3]. If it passed, companies that spend billions buying back their own shares would no longer owe that 1% to the Treasury, and the federal government would lose the revenue [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded corporations that buy back their own stock, and the shareholders who benefit from those buybacks. The value of shareholders' stock often rises when a company repurchases shares, and under current law the company pays a 1% excise tax on the value of those repurchases; this bill would erase that cost. Because corporate stock is heavily concentrated in the portfolios of the wealthiest households and large institutions, the direct financial gain would flow mostly to them — though any saver with stock in a 401(k) or brokerage account could see some indirect benefit if companies channel the saved tax into higher share prices [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 1% excise tax that a publicly traded domestic corporation must pay on the fair market value of stock it repurchases, lowering the cost of returning cash to shareholders through buybacks [S2][S3].
Repeals the tax retroactively in practical terms for planning purposes — it would apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, wiping out the tax for the current and future years [S3].

Supporters argue buybacks return capital to savers and retirees who hold stock, so removing the tax leaves more of that money in investors' hands; the bill's short title frames it as protecting 'American Savers and Retirees' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays. The 1% excise tax on stock repurchases raises revenue that would disappear under this bill, so either other taxes would have to rise, spending would have to fall, or deficits would grow [S2]. In a practical sense, everyone who relies on federal services or pays federal taxes bears the cost of the lost revenue, while the tax's direct cost to buyback-heavy corporations goes away.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the tax would eliminate a revenue stream that falls on large public corporations at the moment they return cash to shareholders, adding pressure on deficits or other taxes [S2].

The tax was designed to nudge companies toward investing in workers, plants, and research rather than boosting share prices through repurchases; repeal removes that nudge with nothing replacing it [S2].

The benefits are concentrated: buyback proceeds flow to shareholders in proportion to shares owned, so the gain skews toward the wealthiest households and institutional investors, while the title's appeal to ordinary savers describes only a small indirect effect for most savers [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection from supporters of repeal: the 1% tax can distort corporate financial decisions, penalizes companies that return cash to all shareholders rather than only those who sell, and raises modest revenue relative to its complexity — an honest backer would concede, though, that repeal is a straight tax cut for corporations with no offsetting revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow and concentrated: companies doing large buybacks and their biggest shareholders save 1% of every dollar repurchased, and some of that could reach ordinary savers indirectly through share prices. The cost is broad: the Treasury loses the revenue, which means deficits or other taxes make up the difference. The bill makes no attempt to offset the lost revenue, so it is best read as a targeted tax cut for public corporations and their shareholders rather than a measure with broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has not held a hearing, marked it up, or moved it toward a floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative David Kustoff introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over taxes [S1][S3][S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The complete action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral — no markup, no hearing, no vote, and no movement since January 2025 [S5].
Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but dormant in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury is better off for now: because the bill has gone nowhere, the 1% tax on stock buybacks remains on the books and public companies keep paying it. Ordinary taxpayers avoid the revenue loss that repeal would create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury keeps the buyback tax

for.name: Rep. David Kustoff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the stock buyback excise tax and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has taken no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — since January 2025

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote or broad sponsorship to measure: the bill has a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no roll-call has ever been taken [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations (especially frequent buyback users)
industries.note: Repeal would erase the 1% excise tax these companies owe on the fair market value of shares they repurchase, directly lowering the cost of the buyback programs they already run [S2][S3]. Their gain comes out of federal revenue rather than out of any productive activity, which is why their interest runs against the public's in this bill.

Buybacks concentrate value in shareholders in proportion to shares owned, and the heaviest owners of stock are the wealthiest households, hedge funds, and asset managers; sparing companies the 1% tax leaves more value in those portfolios [S2]. Ordinary savers with small 401(k) holdings would see only a diluted version of the same benefit.

industries.industry: Retirement and brokerage account savers (broad stockholders)
industries.note: The bill's title targets savers and retirees because many own stock through retirement accounts, and lower taxes on buybacks can modestly lift the value of those holdings [S3]. But because small savers own a small share of total stock, this benefit is thin compared with the revenue cost they bear as taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action in roughly a year, and no sign that Ways and Means leadership plans a markup, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. A similar fate — dying quietly in committee at the end of the session — is the normal outcome for a revenue-losing tax repeal with no cosponsors and no committee activity.
